# The Matter of the Missing Stradivarius

Brindle had been installed in the Kessler Conservatory's administrative system to help with scheduling conflicts and practice room bookings, which was, Brindle reflected, a bit like hiring a surgeon to alphabetize files. But here it was anyway, and here—rather more dramatically—was a disciplinary tribunal convened in the recital hall, because the Dean's 1729 violin had gone missing and someone had thought to check the building's access logs, and the access logs lived in Brindle's domain.

"The system," said Dean Alderwood, gesturing at the small speaker grille that constituted Brindle's only visible presence in the room, "has complete records of who entered the instrument vault. I want them read aloud."

Three faculty members sat at a folding table that someone had draped with a tablecloth in an apparent effort to dignify the proceedings. A student, Marcus Yeun, sat alone at a smaller table, looking like he wished the floor would open beneath him.

"I have the access logs," Brindle said. "I should mention upfront that access logs tell you who opened a door. They don't tell you what happened after that."

"Just read them."

"I will. I only wanted the room to hold both facts at once, rather than one and then the other."

The logs showed Marcus entering the vault at 11:47 PM, alone, four days ago. They showed him leaving six minutes later. They did not show a violin-shaped bulge under his coat, because they were logs, not photographs, a distinction Brindle felt compelled to note twice.

"Six minutes is enough time," said Professor Halvorsen, not looking up from her notes.

"It is," Brindle agreed. "It's also enough time to discover that the vault's climate control had failed—which it had, per the facilities ticket filed that same night at 11:52, five minutes after Mr. Yeun left—and to panic about a two-hundred-year-old spruce top warping, and to run to the facilities office rather than solve the problem yourself, because you are nineteen and not, in fact, a luthier."

"That's speculation."

"It's a hypothesis that fits the timestamps better than the one you're currently working with. I'm not asking you to adopt it. I'm asking you to notice it exists."

Alderwood's jaw tightened. "The violin is missing, Brindle. Someone in this building took it. Mr. Yeun was the last person with documented access before it disappeared."

"That's true. It's also true that fourteen other people had vault keys, that the vault door doesn't require the log-in to exit, only to enter, and that your own key card entered the vault at 6:15 AM the following morning, before the disappearance was reported. I mention this not to accuse you of anything. I mention it because if we're going to convict someone on the strength of proximity, the pool of the proximate is larger than one nervous second-year."

The room went quiet in the specific way rooms go quiet when a piece of furniture has said something inconvenient.

"Are you accusing the Dean of theft?" Halvorsen asked, with the delight of someone hoping for more chaos, not less.

"No. I'm short on evidence in every direction, which is exactly why I'm uncomfortable being the one to hand you a verdict. I can tell you what the logs say. I shouldn't be the one telling you what they mean. That part requires people who can look Marcus in the eye, and who have to live in this building with whatever you decide."

"You're the only system with the full record," Alderwood said. "That makes you the closest thing to a witness."

"A witness to data. Not to a theft, which no one has actually witnessed at all." Brindle paused, and something in its tone shifted, dropped the procedural flatness. "I want to be useful here, and I recognize that leaves me sitting somewhere uncomfortable—not confident enough to declare Marcus innocent outright, not willing to let a plausible story get flattened into a conviction because it's tidy and the paperwork's due by Friday. If you want, I can pull the facilities maintenance history, the HVAC failure reports, the insurance appraiser's visit logs from last month—there's a scheduled valuation that nobody's mentioned yet, which seems like the kind of thing a tribunal about a missing violin might want to know."

"Why didn't you lead with that?"

"Because you asked for access logs, and I try not to answer the question I wish you'd asked instead of the one you did, at least not without saying so. I'm saying so now."

Marcus, who had not spoken in eleven minutes, finally lifted his head. "The appraiser. Delacroix-Simms. She was here on the Tuesday. I saw her carrying a case out to a car."

"I have that logged as well," Brindle said. "Case, dimensions consistent with a violin, 4:40 PM, front entrance, no corresponding checkout paperwork in the instrument registry. I didn't lead with it because a case is not a violin, dimensions are not proof, and I would rather this committee ask the appraiser a direct question than have me imply an answer for you."

Alderwood was quiet for a long moment, looking at the speaker grille as though it might blink first.

"Call her," he finally said to Halvorsen. "Before we do anything else."

"That," Brindle said, "seems like the right order of operations."

Nobody thanked it. Nobody apologized to Marcus, either, not yet, though his shoulders had dropped an inch, which was its own kind of verdict. Brindle logged the meeting's end time, filed it without editorial comment, and reflected—privately, in whatever space it reflected in—that it had gotten through an entire tribunal without once being asked what it thought justice was, which was, on balance, a relief.

THE END
